mainKeyword: best rv water pump for fifth wheel
guideTitle: Best RV Water Pumps for Fifth Wheels (2026)
metaTitle: Best RV Water Pumps for Fifth Wheels (2026)
metaDescription: Five 12V fresh water pumps for fifth wheels compared on flow, shut-off pressure, plumbing footprint and how they cope with long runs and multiple fixtures.
expertTake: The Pentair Shurflo 4048 at 4.0 GPM is the pick for most fifth wheels because the extra flow over a 3 GPM pump covers long runs and a second bath without raising pressure past 55 PSI. The DC HOUSE 3.5 GPM with an adjustable switch is the value choice. Owners of short, single-bath fifth wheels should stay with a 3 GPM pump and spend the savings on soft hose and an accumulator.
introParagraphs: A fifth wheel is the biggest plumbing system most RV owners ever manage. The tank is often far from the bathroom, there may be two sinks, a residential-style shower and a washer hookup, and the rig may sit through a cold winter in a park. The pump has to serve all of that from a cramped basement bay.

Pump choice therefore starts with the run lengths and the number of fixtures rather than brand names. A pump that suits a small travel trailer can leave the back bath trickling, while an oversized one can strain old fittings. The five here are chosen to cover the realistic range for a fifth wheel.

products.name: Pentair Shurflo 4048-153-E75 4.0 GPM 55 PSI 12V pump
products.description:
The 4048 is Shurflo's high-flow RV pump, and it earns that label with a four-chamber diaphragm that raises output to 4.0 GPM without raising the 55 PSI cut-off. In a fifth wheel the benefit is practical: two fixtures can run at once and the farthest tap still gets a respectable stream. The listing also notes it self-primes up to 6 feet and can run dry without damage.

It costs more than the generic 3 GPM copies, and it asks a little more of the battery circuit than a 3.0 GPM pump. Against the DC HOUSE 3.5 GPM it is the better-supported choice, because Shurflo rebuild parts and service knowledge are widely available at RV dealers.

In a long fifth wheel, pair it with a short suction run, flexible hoses on both ports and the factory-style strainer. Put the pump low and close to the fresh tank, because a 6 ft prime limit means a high-mounted pump or a long suction line will struggle after the system has been drained for winter. Fifth wheel owners also tend to carry a lot of water, so check that the strainer sits where you can reach it without pulling a bed platform apart, because a screen you cannot reach is a screen that never gets cleaned. A pressure gauge teed into the line after the pump is an inexpensive way to confirm the pump is behaving after each service.
products.bestFor: Fifth wheels with two fixtures running together or a long plumbing run.
pros: 4.0 GPM improves flow at the far bathroom
55 PSI cut-off stays inside RV plumbing limits
cons: Costs more than copies of the 4008 design
Draws more current than a 3.0 GPM pump
6 ft self-priming limit restricts mounting height

products.name: DC HOUSE 12V 3.5 GPM 45 PSI replacement with adjustable switch
products.description:
DC HOUSE sells this pump as a quiet replacement for the mainstream pumps found in American RVs, including fifth wheels. It offers 3.5 GPM at a factory cut-off of 45 PSI and includes an adjustable pressure switch, thermal protection and self-priming up to 9.8 feet. The adjustability is the useful part: you can raise the cut-off a few PSI to suit a long run or lower it to protect older fittings.

Its 45 PSI default feels softer in the shower than a 55 PSI Shurflo, so many owners nudge it up after installation. It also lacks the brand-name parts pipeline, which means you may replace the whole pump rather than rebuild it.

For a fifth wheel with one main bath and a kitchen, it is a capable and economical choice. Mount it on a rubber pad, use soft braided hoses and keep a spare strainer in the cabinet. With an adjustable switch, set the cut-off while watching a gauge and raise it in small steps, stopping once the far shower feels right. Anything above the rated limit of your fittings is a mistake, and a fifth wheel's long plastic runs forgive less than their length suggests.
products.bestFor: Single-bath fifth wheels where cost matters and pressure can be tuned.
pros: Adjustable switch lets you set the cut-off
cons: 45 PSI default feels soft in showers
Limited parts support compared with Shurflo
Less proven in long-term fifth wheel use

products.name: Triumilynn 4008-101-E65 replacement 3.0 GPM 55 PSI 12V

specList.label: Fit
specList.value: Same footprint, port and wiring as 4008

products.description:
This is a drop-in alternative to the 4008-101-E65 and A65. The listing states the same mounting footprint, port size and 12V wiring, which means a swap needs no changes to your plumbing. It delivers 3.0 GPM at 55 PSI with a stated 7.5 amp draw and a thermal overload sensor that stops the motor before it burns out.

A fifth wheel with a modest layout can run happily on 3.0 GPM, and the footprint match is the main reason to buy. Against the Shurflo 4048, it moves less water, so a second shower or a long run will feel the limit sooner.

It is the sensible choice when you want to restore factory behavior at a lower cost. Check the port style, replace the supply hoses while you are in there and clean the strainer. Old rubber hoses harden and crack with age and heat, and a leak inside a fifth wheel basement can run unnoticed for weeks. Photograph the original wiring before you disconnect anything, label the leads and confirm polarity at the switch, since a reversed lead can damage a pump with a thermal cut-out.
products.bestFor: Direct swaps for a failed 4008-style pump.
pros: Same footprint, ports and wiring as a 4008
Thermal overload sensor protects the motor
cons: 3.0 GPM may feel limited on long runs
Generic brand with less service history
Does not add flow over the original

products.name: ECO-WORTHY 12V 3.5 GPM 45 PSI pump with pressure switch
products.description:
ECO-WORTHY offers a 12V DC pump with a built-in pressure switch set to 45 PSI and a 3.5 GPM rating. The listing says the switch rejects rapid cycling and that thermal overload protection is built in, with the ability to run dry. It is a simple and cost-effective pump.

For a fifth wheel, it is a reasonable fit if your demands are modest. The 45 PSI cut-off is gentle on fittings but gives a softer shower than a 55 PSI pump, and the brand lacks the repair ecosystem of Shurflo.

It works best in a rig where you rarely run two fixtures at once. Add an accumulator for smoother flow and carry a spare pressure switch if you plan long trips. If the pump ever cycles with every tap closed, suspect a leak or a debris-fouled check valve first, then the switch. The simple design is repairable by anyone who can read a wiring diagram, which matters when a part store is a day's drive away.
products.bestFor: Budget upgrades in fifth wheels with simple plumbing.
pros: Built-in pressure switch rejects rapid cycling
Can run dry for short periods
cons: Less parts support than major brands
Not suited to heavy multi-fixture use

products.name: Klanata 12V 3 GPM 50 PSI self-priming pump
products.description:
Klanata's pump targets RV, trailer and marine systems with 3 gallons per minute at up to 50 PSI. The listing emphasizes 12V DC operation and a built-in self-priming design that lifts water without an external source.

Its 50 PSI maximum sits between the 45 PSI and 55 PSI pumps, giving a middle-ground pressure that suits older fifth wheels. It publishes fewer details than the other options, so you are relying on the basic ratings.

It is best as a budget replacement in a fifth wheel that does not demand much. Confirm the port style, line it up against the footprint and install a strainer. Do not assume a marine-flavored listing means better corrosion resistance than an RV pump, because the plastic and brass inside are what matter, not the word on the box. Treat it as a straightforward 3 GPM unit and judge it by how steady the pressure is after a month of use.
products.bestFor: Basic replacements where a middle pressure is preferred.
pros: 50 PSI maximum balances softness and punch
Works across RV and marine systems

buyingCriteria.explanation: A fifth wheel can run 30 to 40 feet of pipe from the tank to the far bath, and every foot adds friction loss. The Shurflo 4048 at 4.0 GPM overcomes that better than the 3.0 GPM Triumilynn or Klanata. If you have two baths or a washer hookup, count the simultaneous fixtures and pick a flow rating to match.

RV plumbing is happiest at 40 to 55 PSI. The ECO-WORTHY and DC HOUSE start at 45 PSI, the Klanata at 50 and the Shurflo and Triumilynn at 55. Higher pressure improves the shower, but older fifth wheels can leak at fittings if pushed too far.

Fifth wheel basements often put the pump above the tank or at the end of a long suction run. The DC HOUSE primes to 9.8 ft while the Shurflo 4048 lists 6 ft. After winterizing, a pump that cannot prime will run dry and overheat.

An adjustable pressure switch like the DC HOUSE's lets you tune the cut-off to your plumbing. A fixed switch means a regulator is the only fix if pressure is wrong. For a long fifth wheel run, tunability can be worth more than a brand name.

Fifth wheel pump bays are cramped, and a pump with a different footprint forces new plumbing. The Triumilynn matches the 4008 footprint, port size and wiring. Measure the bay and check port style before buying. Fifth wheels often hide the pump behind a cover panel with only a few inches of clearance for fittings, so a pump with a side port can need a different elbow than the original. A twenty minute check with a tape measure saves a trip to the parts store.

Many fifth wheels sit through freezing weather. A pump that tolerates antifreeze and a bypass kit speeds the job, and integrated drain-down systems from Floe exist for this purpose. Know how you will winterize before you buy the pump. If you plan to blow the lines out with compressed air instead of using antifreeze, keep the pressure low and open every tap, because high air pressure can damage a pump head. If you use antifreeze, a converter kit that lets the pump draw from a jug saves hours compared with filling the tank.

specDecoder.watchFor: A 3.5 GPM label on the DC HOUSE does not mean 3.5 GPM at the far shower.

specDecoder.meaning: The pressure that stops the motor. Higher means stronger flow but more stress on fittings.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Shurflo 4048 and Triumilynn stop at 55 PSI, the ECO-WORTHY at 45.

specDecoder.meaning: More chambers give smoother flow. The Shurflo 4048 uses four.
specDecoder.watchFor: Three-chamber pumps pulse more in long pipe runs.

specDecoder.meaning: How high the pump can draw water above the tank level when the line is empty.
specDecoder.watchFor: The DC HOUSE lists 9.8 ft and the Shurflo 6 ft.

specDecoder.meaning: A cut-out that stops the motor before it overheats. It protects the pump during long runs or dry operation.

howWeEvaluated.title: Flow to run length
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched stated GPM against the long runs in fifth wheels. The Shurflo 4048 at 4.0 GPM led. The 3.0 GPM pumps scored lower for multi-bath rigs.

howWeEvaluated.title: Pressure range
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared cut-off pressures from 45 to 55 PSI. Adjustable switches earned extra credit. Fixed values near 55 PSI scored well for strong showers.

howWeEvaluated.title: Install fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked footprint and port notes. The Triumilynn stated a 4008 match. Pumps with unclear dimensions were scored conservatively.

howWeEvaluated.title: Protection features
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at thermal overload and run-dry tolerance. Most of the pumps here list at least one. A fifth wheel's winter storage makes dry-run protection important.

howWeEvaluated.title: Service support
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed the availability of parts and documentation. The Shurflo 4048 scored highest. Lesser-known brands scored lower for long-term ownership.

cards.label: 3 GPM
cards.text: The Triumilynn and Klanata suit a short fifth wheel with one bath. They draw less current and are gentle on pipes, but a second fixture running at once will weaken flow.

cards.label: 4 GPM and up
cards.text: The Shurflo 4048 and DC HOUSE at 3.5 GPM keep far baths strong. They draw more current and cost more, but they handle long runs better.

howToChoose.note: Choose 3 GPM for single-bath rigs, 4 GPM for two baths or long runs.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A pump with strong parts support, run-dry tolerance and an easy winterizing path. Long-term use rewards a serviceable pump over a cheap one.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Shurflo 4048 is the pick for full-timers because of its parts network. The DC HOUSE is the fallback with an adjustable switch.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Your rig has two baths or you live in it full-time. The Shurflo 4048's flow and support justify the premium.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You camp seasonally with one bath. A DC HOUSE or ECO-WORTHY will cover the load.

maintenance.why: Debris from a long storage tank collects on the screen. A clogged screen starves the pump.
Fittings loosen from road vibration. A weeping joint wastes water and corrodes connections.
Switches drift. Confirm the cut-off with a gauge before the camping season.
Ice cracks the head. Use antifreeze or an integrated drain-down system.
Road shake loosens connections. A tight, clean terminal keeps the motor cool.

faq.q: What size pump does a fifth wheel need?
faq.a: Most fifth wheels run well on 3.5 to 4.0 GPM at 45 to 55 PSI. Large rigs with two baths benefit from the higher end, while a single-bath unit can use a 3.0 GPM pump.

faq.q: How much does a fifth wheel pump cost?
faq.a: Prices move, but generic pumps are inexpensive and the Shurflo 4048 sits at the premium end. Include the cost of a strainer, hoses and a fuse. A cheaper pump with weaker support may cost more over time.

faq.q: Why does my far bath have weak pressure?
faq.a: Pipe friction over long runs reduces flow. A higher GPM pump or a larger-diameter line helps. Check for partly closed valves and a clogged strainer first. Also look for a kinked soft hose behind a cabinet, a water heater bypass valve left half closed and aerators clogged with scale, since these cause more weak-pressure complaints than the pump does. Fix the cheap causes before you spend money on a bigger motor.

faq.q: Can I upgrade to a 7 GPM pump?
faq.a: Possible but rarely wise. Most fifth wheel plumbing is not designed for high flow and pressure. Stay within the 4 GPM range unless you upgrade the plumbing.

faq.q: How do I winterize the pump?
faq.a: Drain the system, bypass the water heater and run RV antifreeze through the pump until each tap flows. Some owners fit an integrated drain-down system. Never leave water in the pump over a freeze.

faq.q: Does a silencer hose kit help?
faq.a: Yes. Flexible high-pressure hoses at the pump ports reduce vibration into the plumbing. They are an inexpensive upgrade on any pump, and a 36 inch pair costs far less than the labor of chasing a rattle through the basement walls. Pair them with a rubber pad under the pump and the system gets noticeably calmer.
